chapters.title: Hook
chapters.purpose: The highest vaults of the Middle Ages came down; others still stand. Pose the central question.

chapters.title: Stone and its outward push
chapters.purpose: Stone cannot be pulled apart; a vault pushes outward; one Romanesque answer, the barrel-vaulted church; Gothic rearranges the supports.

chapters.title: The pointed arch
chapters.purpose: Taller over the same span, thrust depends on geometry and loads, the hanging chain, not a Gothic invention, level crowns over different widths.

chapters.title: The rib vault
chapters.purpose: In the four-part vault shown, ribs direct the load toward four piers; how vaults stand is debated; the web works too; the wall is no longer the main support.

chapters.title: The flying buttress
chapters.purpose: The thrust is carried outside, over the aisle roof, down to a massive buttress.

chapters.title: Walls of light
chapters.purpose: Why they did it: Saint-Denis, Chartres; was it a revolution or continuity?

chapters.title: Building by geometry
chapters.purpose: Rules from trial and error, ropes and squares, templates, centering, carpenters, little room for error.

chapters.title: The limit: Beauvais
chapters.purpose: Raised beyond its proportions, the vaults fell in 1284; the repair, the tower of 1573; Amiens' iron chain.

chapters.title: Why they stand
chapters.purpose: Stability rather than strength: the line of thrust under its assumptions, what a scaled model does and does not show.

chapters.title: Never impossible
chapters.purpose: Answer the question; not a simple story of progress; call to action; credits.
